newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK -- 2-, 5-yr note auctions.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK -- 2-, 5-yr note auctions.

text.p: The Treasury's two- and five-year note auctions could turn out to be the main market events of the coming week when fresh economic data will be scarce and participants will be waiting for key data due at the end of April and the start of May, analysts said.
The Treasury will sell $17.0 billion in two-year notes on Tuesday and $12.5 billion in five-year notes on Wednesday.
"It's really going to be a very quiet week from the point of view of economic news," said Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc.
Against that backdrop, the Treasury auctions could be the most prominent feature of the week and should attract good demand, he said.
Moran said rates might have to rise a bit from Friday's closing levels to make the bonds more enticing.
In when-issued trade on Friday, the two-year notes were yielding 6.4225 percent and the five-year notes were yielding 6.72 percent.
As far as data due in the coming week are concerned, the market will get March federal budget figures at 1400 EDT/1800 GMT on Monday.

On Tuesday come two weekly reports on department and chain store sales -- the weekly BTM/Schroders chain store sales figure at 0900 EDT/1300 GMT and the Redbook chain store sales figures at 1455 EDT/1855 GMT. Both reports are of interest to the market without being terribly influential, analysts said.
U.S. March import and export prices are also due on Tuesday at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT. This information, also, is unlikely to be a market mover, analysts said.
Wednesday is a day without any fresh data. But Thursday's weekly U.S. jobless claims data ought to be of interest, since claims have risen in each of the last two weeks.

Economists polled by Reuters estimated, on average, that new jobless claims totaled 328,000 in the week ended April 19. That would represent a marginal decline from the 332,000 new claims reported for the week ended April 12 but would be slightly above the 324,000 claims reported a week before that.

Economists said the jobless claims figures reported for the first two weeks of April showed that the labor market was still tight, but not getting tighter. Tight labor markets have concerned Federal Reserve policy makers who worry that scarce labor will push wages -- and eventually prices -- higher.
The Conference Board's Help-Wanted Advertising Index, another gauge of labor market strength, also comes out on Thursday. In February, the index measured 90.0. A forecast for March was not available.

One new piece of information on the interest-rate sensitive housing sector is due on Friday. Sales of existing homes during March occurred at an annualized rate of 4.14 million, down from 4.26 million in February, according to economists polled by Reuters.
The market has garnered good support for itself just above seven percent on the 30-year Treasury bond yield.
But analysts said its potential to rally is limited.

The primary reason for that is that the market is waiting for four closely watched economic reports, all due the following week. The reports are the first quarter Employment Cost Index (ECI), due April 29, the preliminary first-quarter GDP estimate, due April 30, the April National Association of Purchasing Management (NAPM) index, due May 1 and finally, the April U.S. employment report, due on May 2.

Second, the week will feature periodic speeches and remarks of various Fed officials. Even "dovish" Fed officials have lately characterized the U.S. economy as strong. Since the bond market needs signs that economic growth is tapering off in order to move higher, those comments have crimped small rallies and could do so again, analysts said.

Among the Fed officials speaking in the coming week are Fed Vice Chairwoman Alice Rivlin, Richmond Fed President Alfred Broaddus, Chicago Fed President Michael Moskow and Cleveland Fed President Jerry Jordan.
Dealers indicated that Federal funds would open at 5-1/2 percent on Monday.
